title: Probing Geographic World Models in Small vs Large LLMs: Does Scale Improve Linearity?

original_idea.problem: Whether linearity of geographic world models improves with model scale or whether larger models encode geography differently is unknown.
original_idea.direction: Extract residual stream activations from GPT-2, GPT-2-XL, and Llama-3.2-1B. Train linear and nonlinear probes for latitude and longitude. Compare R2 values and peak probe layer.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: if world models become more linearly accessible at scale, larger models may be more interpretable representationally, aiding scalable oversight. The gap is that geographic knowledge is a somewhat narrow domain for drawing broad interpretability conclusions.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: TransformerLens makes activation extraction straightforward. Training linear probes is standard ML. However, working with three different model architectures and understanding residual stream structure requires intermediate ML knowledge. A beginner with guidance could manage this.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Three models, one probing task (lat/lon), linear vs. nonlinear comparison. Clear deliverable: R2 scaling plot. Well-bounded. Data preparation (city sentences) is simple. Achievable in 30hrs.

novelty.reasoning: Gurnee and Tegmark (2023) 'Language Models Represent Space and Time' (ICLR 2024) already probed the Llama-2 family for geographic linear representations across model sizes, showing linear probes recover latitude/longitude and that capability increases with model size. 'On the Scaling Laws of Geographical Representation in Language Models' (arXiv:2402.19406, 2024) directly studies how geographic probe performance scales with model size. The proposed experiment (GPT-2, GPT-2-XL, Llama-3.2-1B with linear vs nonlinear probes for lat/lon) closely replicates existing work with slightly different model choices. The core finding — larger models have more linearly accessible geographic representations — is established.
